meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In any moment of decision, the best thing you can do is the right thing'?
meta.ogDescription: Popularly pinned on Theodore Roosevelt, but his own archive finds no source. The phrasing goes back to journalist Alfred Henry Lewis in 1910.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — traces to journalist Alfred Henry Lewis
answer.authorDates: 1855–1914 · American muckraking journalist who wrote about Roosevelt
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Theodore Roosevelt ever said this — the Theodore Roosevelt Center finds “no known source” for it. The earliest documented wording traces to journalist Alfred Henry Lewis, who in an 1910 piece on Roosevelt wrote “the best thing is to do the right thing; the next best is to do the wrong thing; the worst thing of all things is to stand perfectly still.”

source.excerpt: The best thing is to do the right thing; the next best is to do the wrong thing; the worst thing of all things is to stand perfectly still.
trail: The Theodore Roosevelt Center finds “no known source” to verify the attribution.
Wikiquote lists it as disputed and traces the wording to Alfred Henry Lewis’s 1910 writing in La Follette’s Magazine.
The earliest known crediting of the polished line to Roosevelt is only from a 1995 U.S. Congressional hearing, per Wikiquote.
source.cutTag: ↑ the polished “In any moment of decision…” version is a later reworking of these words
source.excerptNote: Lewis wrote this as his own characterization of Roosevelt’s bias toward action — not as a quotation of anything Roosevelt actually said. The familiar modern wording (“In any moment of decision…”) is a later, smoother reworking.
source.rightsNote: Alfred Henry Lewis’s 1910 wording is in the public domain (pre-1929). The polished modern aphorism now attributed to Roosevelt is of uncertain, later authorship and cannot be sourced to him.

author.name: Alfred Henry Lewis
author.heading: About Alfred Henry Lewis
author.bio: Alfred Henry Lewis (1855–1914) was an American muckraking journalist, lawyer, and novelist, known for exposing Tammany Hall corruption and for his popular Wolfville Western stories. Around 1910 he wrote admiringly of Theodore Roosevelt’s bias for action, coining the “do the right thing… the worst thing is to stand perfectly still” formulation that was later smoothed into a polished aphorism and misattributed to Roosevelt himself.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most common inspirational quotes pinned on Theodore Roosevelt, appearing across quote sites, business books, and motivational posters — yet it appears nowhere in his speeches or writings.

items.why: The Theodore Roosevelt Center states plainly that “no known source can be found to verify the attribution,” and Wikiquote lists it as disputed.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented wording is not Roosevelt’s at all: journalist Alfred Henry Lewis wrote it in La Follette’s Magazine on 28 May 1910, and the polished modern version was linked to Roosevelt only decades later, per Wikiquote.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Roosevelt
lead: The sentiment is a near-perfect match for Roosevelt’s public image — the strenuous life, the man in the arena, action over hesitation — which is exactly why it attaches to him so easily. Ironically, that fit is no accident: Alfred Henry Lewis wrote the original words about Roosevelt, describing his bias for decisive action, so the phrasing was Roosevelt-flavored from the start even though the words were Lewis’s own.
context.detailsSummary: How a description became a quotation
detailsBody: Over the twentieth century the passage was compressed and smoothed into the aphorism now in circulation, and the framing flipped: a journalist’s characterization of Roosevelt became a first-person Roosevelt quotation. The earliest instance Wikiquote finds of the polished line being credited to Roosevelt is a 1995 U.S. Congressional hearing — more than eighty years after his presidency.
context.pull: Lewis was describing Roosevelt’s temperament — not quoting him.
